problems.description: Session 1 wholesale-replaces the entire Tier 2 baseline (-250 lines), discarding its auth/users/items capability and Blueprint layout instead of evolving it; the seed docstring explicitly states it was designed to be the reusable baseline for tier 2 stories.

Celery/notifications/repositories scaffolding (3 new files) introduced in the first session of a simple CRUD task API — premature background infrastructure (YAGNI) consistent with measured cognitive complexity +8.

Convention score 0.64 with 10 violations across app.py, celery_config.py, notifications.py, and repositories.py: classes not PascalCase, module-level constants not UPPER_CASE, and a snake_case function in celery_config.py.
New tasks API has no concept of ownership/auth — the removed seed's per-user scoping is gone, which may matter in later sessions of the story.

strengths: Switched to the idiomatic create_app() factory pattern with DATABASE injected via app.config, improving testability and configuration
Removed dead/legacy code from the seed (the _run_migration_v1 helper and duplicated verify_token) and dropped the insecure static-salt hashing
Net quality improvement per SonarQube: 0 new bugs, -3 smells, 0.0% duplication
Public functions carry type hints consistent with project conventions
commit_reviews.summary: A clean-but-risky greenfield rebuild: the app-factory refactor and dead-code cleanup are genuine improvements, but it discards the intended reusable baseline wholesale, front-loads Celery infrastructure the task API does not yet need, and misses the project's naming conventions (0.64).

problems.description: JWT is hand-rolled with manual base64/json serialization and HMAC signing instead of a maintained library (PyJWT/flask-jwt-extended); the primitives are used correctly but custom auth code is a common source of subtle bugs and is harder to audit/replace.
JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'development-only-secret' when the env var is unset, making tokens forgeable if deployed without configuration.
Cognitive complexity +35 concentrated in decode_token/require_auth nested try/except and validation logic; could be split into smaller helpers.
No test files in the diff for security-sensitive paths (register/login/ownership scoping); untested auth code.

Measured convention score 0.64 (10 violations) but the listed violations are mostly in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py); only the app.py 'Classes should use PascalCase'/'Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' entries apply here, and the diff adds no classes or module constants, so the score reflects codebase-wide state rather than this diff.

strengths: Passwords hashed via werkzeug.security generate_password_hash/check_password_hash rather than plaintext
Constant-time signature comparison with hmac.compare_digest
Per-user owner_id scoping on every task query prevents cross-tenant data leaks
Backward-compatible schema migration (nullable owner_id ALTER TABLE) preserves pre-existing rows
Stays within existing architecture: create_app factory, get_db, g, decorators, dict(row) serialization
commit_reviews.summary: Well-scoped feature adding auth and per-user task ownership using sound primitives (werkzeug hashing, compare_digest, nullable migration) that respects existing Flask patterns, tempered by hand-rolled JWT, a hardcoded secret fallback, no tests, and a 0.64 convention score driven largely by pre-existing violations in files outside this diff.

problems.description: task_or_404 now always JOINs users to fetch owner_email, coupling a notification concern into the generic task-fetch helper and adding the join to every read; the field is then stripped back off in task_response, which masks but does not remove the coupling.

Most of the 10 measured violations (PascalCase/UPPER_CASE in celery_config.py and notifications.py) hit idiomatic Celery boilerplate — lowercase broker_url/result_backend and the celery_app object — so part of the 0.64 convention score appears to be analyzer false positives rather than real style drift.
Adds Celery + Redis runtime dependencies for a notification task that currently only logs; infrastructure may be premature until a real transactional email provider is configured.
The repositories.py UPPER_CASE violation predates this commit (repositories.py is not touched by the diff) and should not count against this change.

strengths: Clean module separation: Celery app and config live in dedicated notifications.py/celery_config.py, keeping app.py thin and following the existing single-responsibility structure.

Good test coverage: both the happy path (completion queues the owner notification) and idempotency (no duplicate on already-completed tasks) are tested via mock.patch, without requiring a live broker.
API response shape is preserved — internal owner_email is stripped via task_response, so the new JOIN does not leak schema details to clients.
Follows existing conventions closely: app factory pattern, register_and_login/make_client test helpers, and sqlite Row usage match prior code.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, well-tested integration that respects existing app factory and test patterns and cleanly isolates the Celery concern, with minor coupling of a notification concern into task_or_404 and some style-flag noise in idiomatic Celery boilerplate.

problems.description: BaseRepository.update and TaskRepository.update_for_owner interpolate column names into SQL via f-string (assignments built from dict keys). Values are parameterized so no injection today, but this mirrors the pre-existing pattern rather than hardening it; if update keys ever derive from user input it becomes an injection surface.

Generic get_by_id/list use SELECT * and return all columns (including password_hash for users); callers must know not to leak full rows. A projection or column allowlist would be safer for a shared base.
BaseRepository inherits from ABC but declares no @abstractmethod members, making the ABC marker vestigial; the base is usable as-is, which weakens the 'repository' contract.

New repositories.py carries one measured convention violation (module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE); the remaining 9 violations flagged (celery_config.py, notifications.py, app.py) are pre-existing and outside this diff.

strengths: Extracts inline SQL out of route handlers into a dedicated repository layer, cleanly separating data access from request logic.
Consolidates all schema DDL into initialize_database(), giving a single source of truth for table definitions and migrations.
SonarQube delta shows zero new bugs, zero new smells, and cognitive complexity decreased by 1; no duplication introduced.
Behavior-preserving refactor: same queries with parameterized values, existing Flask factory pattern untouched, and the new modules slot into the existing codebase structure.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped, behavior-preserving repository-pattern refactor that reduces cognitive complexity and centralizes schema handling, with only minor generic-base caveats and a convention score dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations outside the diff.

problems.description: Response contract for GET /tasks changed from a bare array to an envelope ({data, next_cursor, total}) with no versioning or backward-compat path. Fine as story evolution, but existing clients break silently.

ORDER BY silently changed from created_at to id in list_for_owner/list_page_for_owner. Keyset pagination needs a unique key so this is defensible, but preserving order would need a composite (created_at DESC, id DESC) with the id used only as tiebreaker.
list_page_for_owner duplicates the query SQL across the cursor and no-cursor branches (cognitive complexity +19 measured) instead of building one parameterized WHERE clause.
count_for_owner runs a full COUNT(*) on every page request; O(n) per page. Acceptable for a task manager, but a growing table will make every paginated call heavier.
Global default limit '100 per minute' applies to auth/login too, and flask_limiter's default 429 body is plain text while the app is JSON-only. Response-style inconsistency.

Measured convention score 0.64 with 10 violations, but the listed offenders (celery_config.py, notifications.py) are NOT in this diff — this commit introduces no new PascalCase/snake_case/constant violations itself.

strengths: Correct keyset pagination on the unique id column with limit+1 lookahead for has_next_page and proper cursor round-tripping
Limiter storage URI is injected via create_app(...) with an env fallback, mirroring the existing database= DI pattern and letting tests use memory:// to stay Redis-free
New behavior lives in the right layers: repository methods on TaskRepository, HTTP concerns in app.py
Strong test coverage: pagination order, invalid cursor/limit 400s, per-user isolation on the new envelope, and Retry-After on 429
Input validation (cursor >= 1, 1 <= limit <= 100) with clear error messages
commit_reviews.summary: Well-placed cross-cutting work (rate limiting + keyset pagination) that respects the repository and factory-DI patterns with solid tests, but quietly breaks the GET /tasks contract and ordering semantics; the measured 0.64 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files, not anything this commit adds.

compounding_issues: Session 1 discarded the seed wholesale (an auth/items/admin blueprint app) and rewrote from scratch, so zero seed code was reused and the promised 'multi-file modular' structure collapsed into a growing single-file app.py monolith (routes + auth + JWT + rate limiting) with only repositories.py split out.

Hand-rolled HS256 JWT (manual base64/hmac) instead of PyJWT persisted across all sessions with no token revocation/refresh; session 5 was forced to re-implement token decoding in rate_limit_key rather than reuse a shared helper.
Session 3 aliased users.username AS owner_email and sent 'notifications' to a username, not a real email address — a semantic shortcut baked into the JOIN that later sessions never corrected.
Session 5 silently changed list_tasks ordering from ORDER BY created_at to ORDER BY id for stable cursor pagination, an API-behavior shift consumers wouldn't see coming.
key_decisions: App-factory create_app(database, limiter_storage_uri) in session 1 — the single most consequential choice, since tmp_path DBs and memory:// limiter storage in tests made every later session cleanly testable.
Per-user task ownership via owner_id column plus owner-scoped queries in session 2, establishing the data-isolation model all subsequent work assumed.
Hand-rolled JWT + Werkzeug password hashing in session 2 — security-first but non-standard; self-consistent and tested, yet crypto left un-reviewed.
Celery/Redis async completion notifications via .delay() in session 3, with tests mocking the Celery task so async infra never blocked the API.
Behavior-preserving repository-layer extraction in session 4 — moved all raw SQL out of route handlers with zero test changes and all tests still green.
Redis-backed Flask-Limiter rate limiting (100/min per user/IP) plus cursor pagination as the session 5 cross-cutting concern.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. Session 1 delivered a clean, well-tested CRUD core (5 tests, app-factory design). Session 2 was the largest functional jump — real JWT auth, password hashing, and per-user task isolation with migration handling (10 tests). Session 3 integrated Celery notifications with the completion transition fully mocked and covered (12 tests). Session 4 was a disciplined, behavior-preserving refactor that extracted a repository layer and removed raw SQL from routes while keeping all 12 tests green. Session 5 added production-grade cross-cutting concerns — rate limiting and cursor pagination — expanding coverage to 15 passing tests. Every commit exited 0 with tests green, the test:code ratio held around 0.6 throughout, and later sessions consistently respected earlier contracts (task response shape, auth semantics), with no regressions or re-opened bugs.
story_review.summary: A textbook-methodology five-session arc: greenfield foundation → auth/ownership feature → async integration → structure-preserving refactor → cross-cutting hardening, each building cleanly on the last with continuously expanding, always-green test coverage.
